description: Barber surgeons to Lister's carbolic acid — how treatment of disease changed from c.500 to 1900.
content_html:
Treatment Through the Ages

Treating illness has always been one of humanity’s most urgent concerns. From the herbal remedies of medieval apothecaries to the carbolic spray of Victorian operating theatres, the history of treatment shows both how medical practice changed and how long some ideas persisted. Two of the most important revolutions in treatment — anaesthetics and antiseptic surgery — came within two decades of each other in the mid-nineteenth century, transforming surgery from a desperate last resort into a viable medical option.

Medieval Treatments: Herbal Medicine and the Humours

Medieval physicians treated illness according to the theory of the four humours. If a patient had a fever (too much blood, in this system), a physician might prescribe bloodletting to remove the excess. Bloodletting was performed using leeches or by cutting a vein with a lancet. Herbal medicine was widely used alongside these approaches: plants such as garlic, sage and thyme were prescribed for various conditions, and many were genuinely mildly effective. Women healers and apothecaries often had considerable herbal knowledge, passed down through generations.

Medieval hospitals, often run by the Church, provided rest and nursing care but had little ability to cure disease. Barber surgeons occupied a lower social rank than physicians and performed manual procedures including tooth extraction, wound-setting, the lancing of abscesses and amputation. They had no understanding of infection and operated without anaesthetics or antiseptics, making surgery extremely dangerous. Death from infection after surgery was very common.

Key Fact

Medieval treatments included bloodletting (rebalancing the humours), herbal medicines (varying effectiveness), and surgery by barber surgeons (no anaesthetics, no antiseptics — high death rate from infection). The Church’s influence reinforced the idea that prayer and spiritual care were as important as physical treatment.

Between 1500 and 1700, treatment changed slowly. The work of Andreas Vesalius (1543) and William Harvey (1628) improved understanding of the body’s structure and circulation, but these insights filtered down to treatment only gradually. Herbal remedies remained central. The first London Pharmacopoeia — a standardised list of medicines — was published in 1618, reflecting attempts to systematise herbal treatment. Pharmacopoeia publications helped unify practice, but they still contained many ineffective or harmful remedies.

James Simpson and Anaesthetics, 1847

Before 1847, surgery was performed on conscious patients who had to be physically held down. Speed was the surgeon’s most valued skill; the fastest could amputate a limb in under two minutes. The pain and shock of surgery killed many patients even before the risk of infection. This changed when James Simpson, a Scottish obstetrician working in Edinburgh, began experimenting with anaesthetics.

Simpson had already been using ether to reduce pain during childbirth, but found it unpleasant to administer. In November 1847, he and colleagues experimented with chloroform at a dinner party, inhaling it themselves. They awoke on the floor, having lost consciousness. Simpson immediately recognised its potential. He began using chloroform in his obstetric practice and published his findings that same year. The medical establishment initially resisted, partly on the grounds that pain in childbirth was natural and biblically ordained. Opposition faded significantly when Queen Victoria accepted chloroform during the birth of Prince Leopold in 1853, lending royal approval to the new technique.

Key Fact

James Simpson first used chloroform as an anaesthetic in November 1847. Queen Victoria accepted chloroform during childbirth in 1853, giving royal endorsement to anaesthetics. Anaesthetics allowed longer, more complex surgery but initially increased infection deaths because operations took longer.

Even with anaesthetics, death rates after surgery remained high. In the 1860s, roughly half of surgical patients at major hospitals died from post-operative infection, which surgeons called ‘ward fever’. The solution came from Joseph Lister, a Glasgow surgeon who had read Pasteur’s germ theory. Lister reasoned that if germs caused decay in organic matter, they might also cause infection in wounds. In 1865, he began spraying carbolic acid — a chemical already used to treat sewage — onto wounds and surgical instruments, and soaking dressings in it.

The results were dramatic. In a series of eleven compound fracture cases, Lister lost only two patients; previously the death rate from such injuries had been very high. He published his findings in The Lancet in 1867. Surgeons gradually adopted antiseptic technique, though some resisted for years. By the 1890s, aseptic surgery — preventing germs from being present at all, rather than killing them after entry — was replacing Lister’s antiseptic approach as the standard of care.

The Combined Impact of Anaesthetics and Antiseptics

The combination of anaesthetics (1847) and antiseptic surgery (1865) transformed medicine. Surgeons could now perform longer, more complex operations with patients unconscious and without the previously near-inevitable risk of fatal infection. Death rates from surgery fell sharply in hospitals that adopted both techniques. The shift was not instant: Lister’s methods were resisted in Britain longer than in parts of Continental Europe and the United States. But by 1900, the basic framework of modern surgery — anaesthetised, sterile — was established. Both changes were dependent on advances in knowledge: anaesthetics on chemistry, antiseptics on germ theory.
exam_tip_html: Questions on treatments often ask you to explain a consequence or assess change. When writing about Lister, don’t just describe what he did with carbolic acid — explain the consequence: death rates from surgery fell dramatically, and his work made complex surgery viable for the first time. For a ‘change’ question, remember that anaesthetics and antiseptics both depended on prior scientific advances (chemistry and germ theory respectively) — this links treatment to knowledge and is a strong analytical point.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Medieval treatment was based on bloodletting, herbal medicines and barber surgeon operations — all conducted without anaesthetics or understanding of infection, making surgery especially deadly.
  • James Simpson introduced chloroform as an anaesthetic in 1847, enabling pain-free surgery; Queen Victoria’s use of chloroform in 1853 helped overcome public resistance.
  • Joseph Lister applied germ theory to surgery in 1865, using carbolic acid as an antiseptic to dramatically reduce post-operative infection deaths, establishing the basis of modern surgical practice.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the work of barber surgeons in medieval Britain.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with supporting detail. Example: Barber surgeons performed amputations and wound-setting without anaesthetics, meaning patients had to be physically held down and pain and shock frequently caused death. [2 marks: 1 for feature, 1 for detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of James Simpson's introduction of anaesthetics.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Simpson first used chloroform in November 1847 after experimenting on himself and colleagues; it caused unconsciousness, removing the pain of surgery. Feature 2: Despite initial religious opposition, Queen Victoria's use of chloroform during the birth of Prince Leopold in 1853 gave royal approval and helped overcome resistance. [2 marks per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Joseph Lister's introduction of antiseptic surgery in 1865.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of the consequence (dramatic fall in post-operative infection deaths, enabling complex surgery, transformation of hospital mortality rates) with embedded evidence. Secure: Clear consequence with relevant evidence. Developing: Consequence identified, limited explanation. Emerging: Simple statement that fewer people died. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the discovery of anaesthetics and antiseptic surgery for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (pain-free, infection-reduced surgery) AND over time (foundation of modern surgical practice, enabling increasingly complex operations by 1900 and beyond). Secure: Both dimensions of significance with evidence. Developing: One dimension, limited evidence. Emerging: Description only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Lister's use of antiseptics was more significant than Simpson's use of anaesthetics in improving treatment.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates both sides with evidence — anaesthetics removed pain and fear, made complex surgery possible; antiseptics addressed the greater killer (post-operative infection) and made the surgery survivable. Acknowledges the two developments worked together. Reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: Both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: One side argued with limited evidence. Emerging: Descriptive. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How far did the treatment of disease change between the medieval period and 1900? Use evidence across all three eras to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change across medieval (bloodletting, herbal, barber surgeons), early modern (pharmacopoeia, gradual improvement but no major break), modern (anaesthetics 1847, antiseptics 1865, aseptic surgery 1890s). Weighs change against continuity (herbal remedies still used; bloodletting persisted into 19th century). Substantiated judgement. Secure: Three eras with evidence. Developing: Two eras. Emerging: Single era. [16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What was bloodletting intended to achieve in medieval medicine?
options: Remove excess humours to restore bodily balance
Reduce fever by cooling the blood

knowledge_checks.q: What chemical did Joseph Lister use as an antiseptic spray in surgery from 1865?
James Simpson first used _____ as an anaesthetic in November 1847, allowing patients to be unconscious during surgery.
Barber surgeons performed operations such as amputation without anaesthetics or _____, leading to very high death rates from infection.
Match each person to their contribution to the treatment of disease:
right: Used carbolic acid to prevent post-operative infection
Performed tooth extractions and amputations without anaesthetics
Introduced chloroform to allow pain-free surgery in 1847

flashcard_questions.q: What was bloodletting, and what was it supposed to do?
flashcard_questions.a: Removing blood by cutting a vein or using leeches, to rebalance the four humours.

flashcard_questions.q: What procedures did barber surgeons carry out in medieval Britain?
flashcard_questions.a: Basic operations including tooth extraction, wound-setting, amputation and lancing abscesses, all without anaesthetics.

flashcard_questions.q: When did James Simpson first use chloroform as an anaesthetic?
How did Queen Victoria's role in 1853 help make anaesthetics acceptable?
flashcard_questions.a: She accepted chloroform during childbirth, giving royal endorsement to the new technique.

flashcard_questions.q: What problem did anaesthetics create for surgery before antiseptics were introduced?
flashcard_questions.a: Longer operations meant more exposure to infection, increasing post-operative death rates.

flashcard_questions.q: What chemical did Lister use as an antiseptic from 1865?
What theory inspired Lister's use of antiseptics?
flashcard_questions.a: Pasteur's germ theory — if germs caused decay, they might also cause wound infections.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Lister publish his findings on antiseptic surgery?
What is the difference between antiseptic and aseptic surgery?
flashcard_questions.a: Antiseptic kills germs in wounds; aseptic prevents germs from entering wounds at all.
A standardised book listing medicines and their uses, issued with official authority.

flashcard_questions.q: What were the two main reasons surgery was so dangerous before 1847?
flashcard_questions.a: No anaesthetics (pain and shock) and no antiseptics (near-inevitable infection).

flashcard_questions.q: By what decade had aseptic surgery replaced Lister's antiseptic approach as standard care?

glossary_terms.definition: The practice of removing blood from a patient by cutting a vein or applying leeches, used to rebalance the humours.
Surgeons in medieval and early modern Britain who also cut hair; they performed basic operations such as tooth extraction, wound-setting and amputation.
Substances that cause a reversible loss of sensation, enabling surgery to be performed without pain.
A prepared book listing medicines and their uses, often issued with official authority to standardise pharmaceutical practice.
The use of chemical agents to destroy bacteria in wounds and on surgical instruments, preventing infection.
The practice of preventing bacteria from reaching wounds or surgical sites in the first place, by sterilising equipment, wearing gloves, and maintaining clean environments.
